source_span: we believe this could affect downstream components, like memory, optical, and other components like power management and analog parts in a bear case. We see a risk that ASICs will lose share in a power-constrained environment relative to GPUs
source_chain: A: US data center power demand outstrips supply through 2028 (57 GW gross shortfall, 32 GW net of 'time to power' solutions, 34% of demand) therefore B: power access concentrates among large, credit-worthy hyperscalers/neoclouds, who take 60-95% of global data center capacity coming online, squeezing smaller/less-credit-worthy/international players therefore C: if the shortfall actually bites, the disruption lands downstream — memory, optics, power management/analog parts — and ASICs lose share to GPUs; NOT Nvidia/Broadcom, whom MS stays convicted are not at risk through 2027. Invalidation: MS's own conviction that NVDA/AVGO's chip-placement visibility and the (limited) upside from BTM/nuclear/international expansion keep the leaders insulated even as the shortfall persists.
pulse_chain: A: electricity, not chip orders, is the binding constraint on the AI buildout through 2028 (57 GW gross / 32 GW net shortfall, developers short 32-42 GW, 34-43% of demand) therefore B: power access concentrates among the credit-worthy large cloud/AI-only players, who take 60-95% of global data center capacity therefore C: if power bites, the disruption lands on memory, optics and other small-dollar components, with custom accelerators losing share to general-purpose GPUs, and US compute share is cut to 55% from 60% because overseas expansion can't absorb the shortfall. Invalidation offered: TSM's Thursday 10/15 print, framed as testing whether the binding limit is power (Morgan Stanley's read) or still equipment/memory supply (Goldman's read via the Dell note).
why: The pulse reproduces Morgan Stanley's A-therefore-B-therefore-C chain and magnitudes (57/32 GW, 60-95% concentration, memory/optics/ASIC exposure, 55% vs 60% compute share) without reversing any step or misattributing the argument, and correctly attributes the opposing memory-tightness read to Goldman's Dell note rather than presenting it as Morgan Stanley's own view.
